LESSON GOALS
•	 To understand simple stories and conversations.
•	 To ask and answer questions about familiar topics 
(personal information, clothes, colours, weather, etc.).
•	 To understand and talk about dates and numbers.
•	 To describe people’s appearance.

LESSON PLAN
1.– WARM-UP ROUTINES (13’)
•	 Hello + register + booklets 
•	 Moods, TR#2
•	 After School Activities
•	 My Pet
2.– STORY (PP.7-11) (8’)
Tell the students the second half of the story using the Big 
Book. Please see the section on storytelling in the Warm-Up 
Routines Index. Before telling the second half of the story, it is 
advisable to ask some recap questions such as:

•	 “Where does the family go to have a picnic?” 
“The family goes to the park to have a picnic.”
•	 “What are they playing in the park?” 
“They are playing frisbee.”
•	 “What can’t they find?” 
“They can’t find mum’s purse.”
3.– WORKSHEET: HOW OLD ARE THEY? (P.4) (9’)
How Old Are They?
LANA
MARY
NANCY
DAVE
MATT
KATE
4
MATERIALS
•	 Crayons or pencils
NOTE: if you collected your Ss books during the booklet 
activity, have them ask you for it now by saying, “Can I have 
my book please?”; otherwise, ask them to take it out of their 
bag. Explain the activity before giving out the books/asking Ss 
to take them out since they might get distracted.
This worksheet shows six different characters with a square 
beside them where Ss must write the age of that character. 
To warm up, begin by asking the Ss how old their classmates 
are. If your Ss don’t know how old their classmates are, ask each 
of them, “How old are you?” to which Ss must answer “I’m … 
years old.” Then ask, “Jane, how old is John? Is he ten?” and 
the child must respond either “Yes, he is,” or “No, he isn’t.”. 
Guess incorrectly at first and ask, “Is he younger or older?”. 
Encourage the Ss to respond, “He is younger,” or “He is older.” 
Next, have the Ss take it in turns to ask you about the 
character’s ages. Ss begin by pointing to one of the characters 
and asking you for example, “How old is Mary? Is she sixty-one 
years old?” to which you should respond, “No, she isn’t,” if the 
question is incorrect. Then a different student should ask, “Is 
she younger or older?” and you should answer, “She is older.”. 
Once they have guessed the age correctly, they should all write 
the age in the square beside the character.
Character’s ages
•	 Kate: 2 
•	 Matt: 4
•	 Lana: 17

•	 Dave: 45
•	 Mary: 80 
•	 Nancy: 34 
> Follow-Up
Ask a couple of questions comparing the age of two characters, 
for example, “Is Dave younger or older than Mary?” to which 
the Ss must answer, “Dave is younger than Mary.” 
If time allows, pair the Ss up and get them to compare two 
of the characters based on the structures used in the previous 
example.

5.– ACTIVITY 8: HOW OLD ARE YOU? (8’)
P.3.2
Lisa
P.3.8
15
Lisa
> How to Play
Ss have to guess the age of a character by asking questions.

> Warm-Up
Ask your Ss, “How old are you?”, and encourage them to 
say, “I’m … years old.”
Next, pretend you’re confused and point to a S. Ask the group, 
“Is Jane 40 years old?”, to which they should answer, “No, she 
isn’t.”. Continue by asking, “Is she younger or older?” and let 
them answer, “She is younger.”. Finish by asking them about 
the correct age, “Is she seven?”, and encourage them to answer 
“Yes, she is!”.
Do one more example if needed.
> Main Activity
Ss must guess the age of the different characters. Prepare 
two sets of cards, one with the character’s age (P.3.8) and one 
without (P.3.2). Choose a pair of cards of the same character, 
keep the age card in your hand and put the character card 
face up on the table for the Ss to see. Introduce the activity by 
saying, “Let’s see if you can guess how old the characters are!”
If you take the Nancy card, for example, you can start by 
asking, “How old is Nancy?” and Ss must take it in turns asking, 
“Is she 20 years old?”, for example. You should then respond, 
“No, she isn’t.” and encourage Ss to ask, “Is she younger or 
older?” to which you should respond “She is older.”. When they 
are ready to guess the character’s age, they should ask, “Is she 
… years old?”. Once the Ss have guessed correctly, show the 
card with the age of the character and let one of the Ss have 
a turn at choosing a card.
> Follow-Up
Show the character cards without the age and ask, “Do you 
remember how old Michelle is?” to which Ss should answer, 
“Michelle is thirty-three years old.”. Try to let each S participate 
at least once.
6.– ACTIVITY 4: PLAY DETECTIVE (8’)

> How to Play
One S is the detective and has to wait outside the classroom 
while another S (the thief) takes the Purse cutout and hides it 
by putting in their pocket or sitting on it. The detective has to 
find out who the thief is by asking questions.
> Main Activity
Introduce the activity by saying, “Let’s see if the detective 
can find the thief!”
Choose a thief, have them hide the purse, and tell the detective 
to come back into the room. Use the structure: “Detective, 
detective, come in!”. The detective should ask questions to 
the group to find out who has the purse.
Before starting the round, the group can say, “What does the 
thief look like?” (they can sing this part). Then the detective 
can start asking yes or no questions such as:
•	 Has the thief got long hair?
•	 Is the thief wearing black shoes?
•	 Is the thief tall or short?
Always insist that the Ss ask and answer questions in full 
sentences and structures. Discourage the Ss from asking 
whether the thief was a boy or a girl unless they really can’t 
figure out who the thief is, because doing so may make guessing 
who the thief is too easy. 
When the detective is ready to guess, they should ask, “John, 
are you the thief?” and the S being accused should respond, 
“Yes, I am.” or “No, I am not.” If the detective accuses somebody 
wrongly, the thief wins; if the detective accuses somebody and 
their guess is correct, then they win.
> Variation
Once Ss are comfortable playing this game, you can bring 
in some props and have the Ss wear different accessories like 
hats and glasses to make it more fun. This way the detective 
can ask a greater variety of questions. 
NOTE: the first few times you play this game, the Ss might 
need your help. Do not hesitate in helping your Ss complete 
some of the sentences or modelling an example and having 
them repeat the sentence after you.

7.– ACTIVITY 9: CLOTHING MEMORY (9’)
P.3.9
> Warm-Up
Quickly review the vocabulary by taking one of the wardrobes 
(P.3.9) and saying, for example, “Look at my wardrobe! It’s full 
of clothes. There is a green T-shirt, a pair of blue jeans, a red 
tie, a blue, white and red cap and a pair of brown shoes.” 
Then give one wardrobe to one of the Ss and say, “Oh! Your 
wardrobe is also full of clothes. What’s in your wardrobe?” 
to which the S should reply, “In my wardrobe there is a purple 
dress, a red coat, a pair of black trousers, a pair of black 
boots and a pair of brown sandals.”. Do the same with one 
or two more Ss.
> Main Activity
The Ss should find matching wardrobes. Place the playing 
cards (P.3.9) face down on the table. When Ss find two matching 
cards, they should say for example, “In both wardrobes, there 
is a white and pink skirt, a green and purple dress, yellow 
knickers, blue flip flops and a pair of pink trainers.”
If they don’t get a pair they should then say, “In this wardrobe, 
there is a white and pink skirt but, in this wardrobe, there isn’t 
a white and pink skirt. They are not a pair.” Each S should at 
least have a turn turning over a pair of cards.
> Follow-Up
To follow up, take a couple of wardrobe cards and describe 
them as a group. Point at the clothing items to elicit the same 
structure from Ss. For example: “In this wardrobe, there is a 
black jacket, a green purse, a pair of yellow knickers, a blue 
dress, and a pair of red trainers.”

BONUS
ACTIVITY 10: DESCRIPTIONS SONG (TR#17)
> Main Activity
Stick up the individual blonde, black, long, short, curly and 
straight hair cutouts on the whiteboard or place them on the 
table before you play the track. For the eyes and mouth, you 
can just use gestures. 
Every time you sing “Are you…?” hold up the palms of your 
hands in the air and then point in front of you when you say 
“You”. Then, perform the action as indicated in brackets below.
DESCRIPTIONS SONG
Are you young? 
(smile and imitate rocking a baby in your arms)
Are you old? 
(bend over and walk as if you are an elderly person with 
a walking stick)
Are you short? 
(put your hands down low)

Or are you tall? 
(put your hands up high)
Have you got big eyes?
(point to your eyes and make a big circle with your hands)
Or have you got small eyes?
(point to your eyes and make a small circle with your hands)
What do you look like? 
(point to anybody)
Tell me something more, I’d like to know! 
(point to yourself first and then hold up your hands 
indicating that you don’t know)
Have you got blonde hair? 
(point to the cutout)
Have you got black hair? 
(point to the cutout)
Is it long or short, curly or straight?  
(point to the cutouts) 
What do you look like? I think I know! 
(put your palms facing up then to your eyes and finish 
by pointing to your head)
ACTIVITY 11: NUMBERS (VERSION 2)
P.E.M.3
55
This game is based on the traditional game Snap!
Mix the Numbers (P.E.M.3.) with the jokers by getting the Ss 
to say, “Mix, mix, mix” and encouraging them to say “Stop!”
Take the whole deck and start turning over the cards and 
putting them in the middle. The Ss should state whatever number 
comes out by saying, for example, “It’s number 62.”. Whenever 
a joker is turned over, they should say, “Snap!”. Try to keep a 
good pace so that the game is more interesting.
The first S to say, “Snap!” gets all the cards in the middle, and 
the next round starts. The game is over when it’s not possible 
to put more cards in the middle. The winner is the S with the 
most cards.
